subject: history
displayName: KS3 History — Victorian Society & Public Health
subtitle: Life in Victorian Britain — poverty, public health reforms, and the growth of cities.

data.targetWord: the health and wellbeing of a whole community, including clean water, sanitation, housing conditions, disease prevention and the removal of waste

examples.en-GB: Public health became a major political issue in Victorian Britain as cholera and other diseases spread rapidly through overcrowded towns.

data.targetWord: a serious disease causing severe diarrhoea and dehydration, which spread rapidly through water contaminated with human waste and killed thousands in Victorian towns

examples.en-GB: Britain suffered major cholera outbreaks in 1832, 1848–49, 1853–54 and 1866, forcing politicians to take public health more seriously.

data.targetWord: the incorrect belief that disease was caused by bad smells or poisonous air rising from rotting matter; though wrong about cholera, believers in miasma still supported cleaning campaigns that could improve public health

examples.en-GB: Miasma theory led many Victorians to campaign for the removal of rubbish and improvement of drainage, even though bad smells were not the actual cause of cholera.

data.targetWord: the scientific idea that some diseases are caused by tiny living microorganisms, which can spread between people through water, food, air or direct contact

examples.en-GB: Germ theory developed in the later nineteenth century and explained why clean water, sewage treatment and hygiene could prevent diseases like cholera.

data.targetWord: a Victorian civil servant and reformer whose 1842 report on the sanitary conditions of the labouring population used statistics to argue that poor sanitation caused disease and that public health reform would save money

examples.en-GB: Edwin Chadwick's 1842 report helped turn public health into a national political issue, though he still believed in miasma theory rather than germ theory.

data.targetWord: a Victorian doctor who investigated the 1854 cholera outbreak in Soho by mapping deaths around the Broad Street water pump, helping demonstrate that cholera spread through contaminated water rather than bad air

examples.en-GB: John Snow's mapping of cholera deaths around the Broad Street pump showed a pattern that supported the contaminated water explanation of cholera.

data.targetWord: systems for keeping places clean and healthy, especially sewers, drains, toilets and waste disposal; improving sanitation was a major goal of Victorian public health reform

examples.en-GB: The 1875 Public Health Act made local councils responsible for sanitation, including sewers, drainage, clean water and street cleaning.

data.targetWord: the event in the summer of 1858 when the polluted River Thames produced such a terrible smell near Parliament that it became impossible to ignore, helping push forward the construction of London's sewer system

examples.en-GB: The Great Stink of 1858 is an example of how a dramatic event could force politicians to act on a problem they had long postponed.

data.targetWord: the Victorian engineer who designed and oversaw the construction of London's major sewer system in the 1860s and 1870s, which redirected sewage away from the Thames and helped reduce waterborne disease

examples.en-GB: Joseph Bazalgette's London sewer system is a major example of how engineering could solve a public health crisis.

data.targetWord: too many people living in a small space; a major problem in Victorian industrial towns where rapid population growth was not matched by adequate housing

examples.en-GB: Overcrowding in Victorian slums meant that disease could spread very quickly through shared water pumps and blocked drains.

data.targetWord: an institution where poor people could receive basic food and shelter in return for work, deliberately designed with harsh conditions to discourage people from seeking poor relief unless truly desperate

examples.en-GB: The workhouse system created by the 1834 Poor Law Amendment Act was widely criticised for punishing poverty rather than addressing its causes.

data.targetWord: the major Victorian law that made local councils legally responsible for providing clean water, sewers, drainage, street cleaning and disease prevention, transforming public health into a normal duty of local government

examples.en-GB: The 1875 Public Health Act was much stronger than the 1848 Act because it made public health duties compulsory rather than voluntary for local councils.

data.targetWord: the voluntary giving of money, time or support to help others, often through charities; Victorian philanthropists funded hospitals, model housing, schools and soup kitchens but could not replace the need for national reform

examples.en-GB: Victorian philanthropy helped some working-class people, but charity alone could not remove the structural causes of poverty and poor health.

data.targetWord: the Victorian idea, popularised by Samuel Smiles, that individuals could improve their lives through hard work, discipline, saving and education; critics argued it ignored structural causes of poverty

examples.en-GB: Samuel Smiles's book 'Self-Help' (1859) promoted the idea that hard work and character could lift people out of poverty, but critics said it blamed the poor for their own situation.

data.targetWord: the law that allowed school boards to build elementary schools in areas where there were not enough places, beginning the process of creating a nationwide system of elementary education

examples.en-GB: The 1870 Education Act began creating school boards to fill gaps in provision, but schooling only became compulsory for younger children in 1880.

data.targetWord: the process of towns and cities growing rapidly as more people move into urban areas in search of work, a major feature of Victorian Britain driven by industrialisation

examples.en-GB: Rapid urbanisation in Victorian Britain created serious problems because housing, water supplies and sewers could not keep pace with population growth.

data.targetWord: a very poor urban area with overcrowded, badly built or unhealthy housing, lacking basic amenities such as clean water, proper drainage or adequate ventilation

examples.en-GB: Victorian slums often had back-to-back housing with shared outdoor toilets, polluted wells and rubbish-filled courtyards that helped diseases spread.

data.targetWord: a key Victorian value, especially among the middle classes, involving being seen as hard-working, sober, orderly, religious and morally responsible

examples.en-GB: Victorian ideas of respectability could encourage positive values like education and saving, but could also lead to blaming poor people for poverty caused by low wages or unemployment.

data.targetWord: an early law that allowed local boards of health to be set up in areas with high death rates, but had limited impact because much action was voluntary rather than compulsory

examples.en-GB: The 1848 Public Health Act was a first step, but many towns did not act because the law was largely voluntary and ratepayers opposed higher local taxes.

data.targetWord: the process by which manufacturing moved to factories using machines and steam power, transforming the British economy and creating rapidly growing industrial cities in the Victorian period

examples.en-GB: Industrialisation in Victorian Britain created new wealth but also serious problems of pollution, dangerous working conditions and overcrowded towns.

data.targetWord: laws passed by Parliament; Victorian public health legislation gradually shifted responsibility for sanitation and disease prevention from individuals to local and national government

examples.en-GB: Victorian legislation on public health, education and factory conditions gradually improved life for many working-class people, though progress was uneven.

data.targetWord: a Victorian nurse and health reformer who used statistics and evidence to improve hospital hygiene and nursing standards, becoming a symbol of Victorian reform

examples.en-GB: Florence Nightingale used careful data collection to show that improved hygiene in hospitals could dramatically reduce the death rate among soldiers.

data.targetWord: councils and local authorities responsible for services such as roads, sewers, water supplies, schools and street cleaning; the 1875 Act made public health a standard duty of local government

examples.en-GB: Victorian local government became increasingly important as councils were given legal duties to provide clean water, sewers and other public health services.

data.targetWord: being unable to afford basic needs such as food, shelter, clothing, warmth and medical care; in Victorian Britain, poverty was widely debated, with some blaming individual behaviour and others pointing to structural causes like low wages

examples.en-GB: Victorian poverty was often caused by low wages, unemployment, illness and high rents rather than by laziness, though many middle-class Victorians preferred to blame the poor themselves.

data.targetWord: a law limiting women and young people working in textile factories to a maximum of ten working hours per day, one of several Victorian Factory Acts that gradually improved working conditions

examples.en-GB: The Ten Hours Act 1847 was a victory for reformers like Lord Shaftesbury who campaigned to limit the exploitation of women and children in factories.

data.sentence: The incorrect belief that disease was caused by bad smells or poisonous air was called ____ theory.
The scientific idea that tiny organisms could cause and spread disease was called ____ theory.
Edwin Chadwick published his major report on sanitary conditions in ____.
John Snow investigated cholera deaths in Soho in 1854 and found many clustered around the ____ water pump.
The terrible smell from the polluted River Thames near Parliament in 1858 was known as the Great ____.
The engineer ____ designed London's major sewer system in the 1860s and 1870s.
The ____ Public Health Act made local councils legally responsible for sewers, clean water and street cleaning.
The 1848 Public Health Act had limited impact because much of the action it allowed was ____ rather than compulsory.
An institution where poor people received food and shelter in return for work, deliberately kept harsh to deter claims, was called a ____.
The ____ Education Act of 1870 allowed school boards to build schools where there were not enough places.
Elementary education became compulsory for children aged 5-10 in ____.
Samuel Smiles's 1859 book '____' promoted the idea that hard work and character could help individuals rise out of poverty.
The rapid growth of cities as people moved in search of factory work was called ____.
Cholera often spread through water ____ with human waste, rather than through bad air as miasma theory claimed.
One argument used to persuade middle-class people to support public health reform was that disease could spread from ____ districts to wealthier areas.
Victorian Britain lasted from ____ to 1901, covering Queen Victoria's reign.
The ____ argued that healthy workers would be more productive and that public health reform would save money in the long term.

data.title: Put the key events of Victorian public health reform in chronological order
items: First major cholera epidemic in Britain (1832)
Chadwick's report on sanitary conditions published (1842)
1848 Public Health Act — voluntary boards of health allowed
John Snow investigates cholera around the Broad Street pump (1854)
Great Stink forces Parliament to act on London's sewers (1858)
Bazalgette's London sewer system built (1861–1875)
1875 Public Health Act — councils given compulsory duties
Elementary education becomes compulsory for ages 5–10 (1880)

data.title: Order the causes of poor public health in Victorian towns from long-term structural to immediate
items: Industrialisation drives rapid movement of people to towns
Housing built quickly without adequate planning or facilities
Overcrowding means many families share small spaces
Shared outdoor toilets near water sources create contamination risk
Blocked drains and open sewers in yards and streets
Polluted water pumps and wells used for drinking water
Disease such as cholera spreads rapidly through contaminated water
High death rates, especially among babies and young children

data.title: Order the education reforms of the Victorian period
items: Churches and charities provide some schools, but access is uneven
1870 Education Act allows school boards to build schools where lacking
1880: Elementary education made compulsory for children aged 5–10
1891: Elementary education made free in most state schools
